question.text:
Consider an unordered array of N distinct integers. What is the minimum number of comparisons required to identify all elements except the largest?

  1. N - 1
     
  2. N - 1 + $\lceil \log_{2} N \rceil$
     
  3. N - 1 + $\lfloor \log_{2} N \rfloor$
     
  4. N + $\lceil \log_{2} N \rceil - 2$

Let $A$ be a one-dimensional array of $n$ distinct real numbers such that $A[i]=f(i)$, where $f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ is an arbitrary but well-behaved function. It is known that:

  • $f(x)$ is continuous and differentiable in the closed interval $[a, b]$,
     
  • $f(x)$ has exactly two real roots in $[a, b]$,
     
  • There exists a unique point $p \in[a, b]$ such that:

$$
\lim _{h \rightarrow 0^{+}} f^{\prime}(p+h)<0, \quad \lim _{h \rightarrow 0^{-}} f^{\prime}(p-h)>0, \quad \text { and } f^{\prime}(p)=0
$$
Given that the array $A$ is indexed over integers in $[a, b] \cap \mathbb{Z}$, what is the minimum time complexity (in terms of $n$ ) required to find the index $i$ closest to the point $p$ where $f(x)$ achieves its maximum value?

  1. $\theta(logn)$
     
  2. $\theta(n)$
     
  3. $\theta(1)$
     
  4. $\theta(log^2(n))$

$\mathrm{f}(\mathrm{n})$ is $\mathrm{O}(\mathrm{g}(\mathrm{n}))$ if there exists some values c , $n_o$ $>0$ such that $\mathrm{f}(\mathrm{n}) \leq \mathrm{c}(\mathrm{g}(\mathrm{n}))$ for all $\mathrm{n} \geq$ $n_o$.

  4. $\mathrm{g}(\mathrm{n})$ cannot be $\mathrm{O}(1)$

Consider the Code fragment of code written in C:

Int bar(int n){
    if(n <= 10){
        return 0;
    }
    if( n < 100){
        Int r = 0;
        for(int i = 0; i < n; i + +){
            r++;
        }
        return r;
    }
    return bar(n/3) + bar(n-1);
}


What will be the recurrence relation for the running time complexity of function $\operatorname{bar}(\mathrm{n})$, where n is in power of $2$ ?


  1. $$
    T(n)= \begin{cases}0 & n \leq 10 \\ c_{2} n & n<100 \\ T\left(\frac{n}{3}\right)+T(n-1)+c_{3} & \text { otherwise }\end{cases}
    $$

  2. $$
    T(n)= \begin{cases}0 & n \leq 10 \\ T\left(\frac{n}{3}\right)+T(n-1)+c_{2} n+c_{3} & n<100\end{cases}
    $$

  3. $$
    T(n)= \begin{cases}0 & n \leq 10 \\ T\left(\frac{n}{3}\right)+T(n-1)+c_{2} n+c_{3} & \text { otherwise }\end{cases}
    $$

  4. $$
    T(n)= \begin{cases}0 & n<=10 \\ c_{2} \log _{3}(n) & n<100 \\ T\left(\frac{n}{3}\right)+T(n-1)+c_{3} & \text { otherwise }\end{cases}
    $$

Which of the following statements is/are FALSE?

  1. If all edge weights of $\mathrm{G}=(\mathrm{V}, \mathrm{E})$ are distinct, the MST of a graph G is unique.
     
  2. Removing the maximum-weight edge in MST always disconnects the graph $\mathrm{G}=(\mathrm{V}, \mathrm{E})$.
     
  3. For a weighted connected undirected graph $\mathrm{G}=(\mathrm{V}, \mathrm{E})$, if any subgraph Gk (formed by removing edge weight k and larger) is disconnected, then MST of G always contains only edge weights $<=\mathrm{k}$.
     
  4. In any MST of a connected graph $\mathrm{G}=(\mathrm{V}, \mathrm{E})$, the number of edges is always exactly $|\mathrm{V}|-1$.

Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?

  2. Let T be a depth -first search tree of an undirected graph G . Let ( $\mathrm{x}, \mathrm{y}$ ) be an edge of $G$ that is not an edge of $T$, then one of $x$ or $y$ is an ancestor of the other.
     
  3. If an edge ( $\mathrm{u}, \mathrm{v}$ ) in an undirected graph G is not a part of the DFS tree and neither $u$ is an ancestor of $v$ nor $v$ is an ancestor of $u$ in the DFS tree, then the edge ( $u, v$ ) is a cross edge.
     
  4. In a DFS if vertex $u$ is discovered before vertex $v$ then there is an edge ( $u, v$ ) in $G$ and either $u$ or $v$ are ancestors of others in the DFS tree.
